claims.text: TaVCrW is initially a disordered BCC solid solution with possible short-range order.
The initial TaVCrW system is modeled with a standard EAM potential.
A Moment Tensor Potential can be trained on DFT data and substituted for the EAM reference potential.
Free energy perturbation can replace thermodynamic integration for calculating the liquid-solid free-energy difference.
An MTP that reproduces the ab initio phase-space distribution provides the structural mediator needed for accurate FEP.
Short-range order stabilizes the TaVCrW solid by approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
Capturing the SRO stabilization energy is critical for accurate free-energy estimation in complex liquids.
The MTP acts as a computationally efficient surrogate for DFT.
The MTP retains sufficient electronic-structure accuracy to represent SRO and electronic-excitation effects.
An EAM potential may fail to capture the SRO stabilization and relevant electronic effects.
A gap in the density of states at the Fermi level can shift the melting point by tens of kelvin.
FEP uses sampling from the accurate MTP to estimate free-energy differences directly and thereby avoids the slow convergence of TI.
The MTP-FEP method will reduce total computational cost by more than 80% relative to TOR-TILD.
The MTP-FEP free-energy error will be less than 0.5 meV/atom relative to TOR-TILD.
The MTP-FEP melting temperature will be within 10 K of the TOR-TILD result.
The MTP must be trained on configurations spanning 2000-2400 K.
Supercells sufficiently large to capture SRO can be validated by reference to the 40,000-plus-atom capabilities of NES or OTIS.
Empirical GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules fail for V and Cr at 0 K and may propagate systematic errors into the MTP.
Neglected high-temperature magnetic fluctuations may become important enough to invalidate the method.
The method is falsified if its error exceeds 0.5 meV/atom, its speedup is below 80%, or its melting point differs by more than 20 K without physical justification.
